title: Pentagon Locks 850 F-35s Into a Decade-Long Deal — and Copenhagen Buys Its First Missile That Can Hit Back
subhead: The Department of War and Lockheed Martin signed a 10-year framework covering at least 850 U.S. F-35s and $7 billion of company-funded investment, while Denmark ordered Kongsberg JSM and Covenant Anthem missiles to build a retaliatory strike capability from scratch. Neither is a contract yet, and that is the story.

sections.heading: The F-35 Multiyear Framework: 850 Jets, $7 Billion From Lockheed, No Price Tag
sections.body:
The Department of War and Lockheed Martin announced a 10-year framework agreement on Thursday covering at least 850 U.S. F-35s across Lots 21-30, plus initial spares, ten years of modification kits and sustainment, and international customer orders. Lockheed said production continues at 156 aircraft per year (Defense News, Lockheed Martin release).

The headline concession runs the other way: Lockheed will self-fund at least $7 billion in program initiatives, according to the Pentagon release. Lockheed CEO Jim Taiclet framed it as the upside of certainty — 'we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain.' Undersecretary for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael Duffey said the deal 'aligns financial incentives with actual performance,' though neither side described what those incentives are.

The arithmetic: 850 jets over 10 years averages 85 U.S. aircraft a year, which matches the FY27 budget request. In FY26, Congress funded 47.

Nothing is signed. No total value, no per-jet price. The framework becomes a contract only if Congress grants multiyear authority and appropriates the money. The House NDAA passed in July and permits multiyear F-35 contracting; Senate Democrats blocked their version in July and leaders have pushed it past the November midterms. A continuing resolution runs through Dec. 11 and bars new multiyear starts.

The readiness backdrop is the reason this exists at all: a GAO report in June found the F-35 mission-capable rate fell from 67% in FY21 to 44% in FY25, with full-mission capability dropping from 38% to 25%. Program chief Lt. Gen. Gregory Masiello told senators the fleet had outgrown its support system.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the Pentagon's third framework-style bet in ten months, after PAC-3 MSE and THAAD. The pattern is consistent: industry puts capital at risk up front, government promises volume it cannot yet fund. If the NDAA stalls again, Lockheed's $7 billion becomes a write-off conversation and the model loses credibility with every other prime watching.

sections.heading: Denmark Buys a Missile That Can Hit Back
sections.body:
Copenhagen will buy two long-range precision-strike missiles — the air-launched Kongsberg Joint Strike Missile for its F-35s and the ground-launched Covenant Anthem — Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus announced Thursday. Quantity, cost and delivery dates were not disclosed, according to TV2's coverage of the ministry press conference.

The driver is explicit and unusual in how openly it is stated: Denmark owes NATO a long-range strike contribution by 2030, and Danish officials cite uncertainty about U.S. support for such weapons under Trump as a reason for urgency (Defense News). Bruus called the buys 'a significant step toward improving Denmark's self-defense capabilities, strengthening NATO, and enhancing our capacity to strike back.'

The Anthem element carries the interesting industrial detail. The missile has never seen combat. Covenant opened a production site in Leipzig, Germany last month and claims output can start there in early 2027; Reuters has reported a target unit price in the mid-six figures once serial production runs. The German defense ministry has so far confirmed only that talks are underway.
sections.whyItMatters: A country of six million people with no long-range strike history is buying retaliation in a box — and pairing a Norwegian-developed, F-35-integrated missile with an untested American startup round. If Anthem performs, Covenant becomes the reference case for Europe's cheap-strike-missile market. If it slips, Denmark has spent political capital on a brochure.

sections.heading: Turkey, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia Sign the Badr MoU in Doha
sections.body:
Defense ministers from four countries signed the Badr Memorandum of Understanding in Doha, covering joint military production, technical training and research and development, Reuters reported and The Defense Post confirmed. The signatories were Turkish Minister of National Defense Yaşar Güler, Qatar's Deputy PM and Minister of State for Defense Affairs Sheikh Saud bin Abdulrahman bin Hasan Al Sani, Indonesia's Deputy Defense Minister Yusuf Jauhari and Pakistan's Minister of Defense Khawaja Muhammed Asif.

The four-way grouping is the substance, not the text. It links a NATO member with an industrial base (Turkey), a Gulf financier (Qatar), a nuclear-armed South Asian army with manpower (Pakistan), and Southeast Asia's largest economy and most active arms buyer (Indonesia). Turkey's drone and missile industry is the most plausible production supplier to all three.

As a memorandum rather than a contract, it commits nobody to money. Reuters reported Ankara's announcement without project-level specifics.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a defense-industrial grouping built entirely outside the US and European export-control regimes, and it does not map onto any existing alliance. Watch for Baykar and Roketsan follow-on announcements — if the MoU turns into co-production lines in Indonesia or Pakistan, the technology-transfer terms become the thing Gulf and Asian buyers benchmark against Western offers.

sections.heading: Britain's Nuclear Deterrent Has a Frigate Problem
sections.body:
The UK Defence Committee's High North inquiry, published Thursday, found a 'serious anti-submarine warfare gap': the Royal Navy has five Type 23 ASW frigates against a requirement of eight, and analysis suggests the number with towed array sonar could stay at five for three more years.

Why it matters beyond fleet math: those frigates screen the Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines transiting in and out of Faslane — the sea leg of the UK's nuclear deterrent. The committee also warned that a lack of under-ice capability limits the Navy's ability to contest Russian freedom of action in the High North, risking a more defensive posture.

The committee put a direct shot across the export bow: if two UK-ordered Type 26 frigates go to Norway to meet its 2030 delivery deadline, the Royal Navy would not reach eight towed-array frigates until 2037. Its finding — 'export success must not come at the expense of the Royal Navy's own Type 26 frigate delivery timelines' — is aimed squarely at BAE Systems and the government's export-first framing. Eight Type 26s are on order from BAE, lead ship due in service 2028; Norway committed to buy five in a 2025 deal worth roughly $14 billion.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the cleanest current example of the tension running through European naval procurement: the same scarce hulls and skilled labor serve either the national fleet or the export customer, not both. Norway's order is a diplomatic win and a scheduling liability, and the committee has now put a date — 2037 — on the cost.

sections.heading: Ukraine Gets a NATO Procurement Account — and a Way Around Washington
sections.body:
NATO will let Ukraine buy weapons, ammunition and equipment through the NATO Support and Procurement Agency, the Financial Times reported Thursday, a move Defense News characterized as potentially faster and cheaper access to defense supplies.

NSPA's director of support to operations, Jacqueline Borsboom, described it as giving Kyiv 'a more structured framework to leverage a broad range of capabilities that we offer: procurement expertise, support services and access to established industrial base.'

The context is a deteriorating US-Ukraine supply relationship: Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia this month, Starshield bandwidth was restricted, and some intelligence sharing was disrupted. Zelensky said a meeting in Oslo on Tuesday agreed to resolve the Starshield and intelligence issues.
sections.whyItMatters: Channeling Ukrainian purchases through NSPA shifts a share of Kyiv's buying from bilateral US Foreign Military Sales to a multilateral European-administered pipeline. That is a structural change in who sets price and priority — and it hands European suppliers a customer relationship they would not otherwise have secured this quickly.

sections.heading: The Barrel Bottleneck: Army Opens 155mm Tube Production to Outside Bidders
sections.body:
The US Army is soliciting new manufacturers for 155mm howitzer barrels, with a sources-sought notice closing Nov. 23. The requirement: capacity to produce up to 10 barrels per month within three years, plus a cost estimate for an initial production run of 40 cannon tubes (Defense News, citing the SAM.gov notice).

Bidders must demonstrate chrome bore coating on steel tubes up to 30 feet long and 7,500 pounds, plus boring, milling, rifling and heat-treatment capability.

The reason is single-source fragility: the Army makes all large-caliber barrels for howitzers and tanks at the Watervliet Arsenal in New York, an 1813-vintage facility. A 2024 Pentagon budget document, cited via The War Zone, said Ukraine's M777 use created demand for more than 30 M776 tubes per month and conceded Watervliet could not keep up. The Army is separately evaluating replacing the M777 with a weapon based on Korea's K9 howitzer.
sections.whyItMatters: The munitions buildout of the past three years focused on shells and rocket motors; barrels were the forgotten consumable, and they wear out faster than anyone planned. Adding private barrel capacity is cheap compared with the alternatives, but it also puts a question mark over Watervliet's long-term role — a subject no one in the Army wants to raise in an election year.

sections.heading: Smaller Signals: Swedish Anti-Jam, Dutch On-Call Production, RAF to Saudi Arabia
sections.body:
Sweden awarded Raytheon UK contracts for Landshield and Landshield Plus GPS anti-jamming systems, with values and platform assignments undisclosed. Landshield uses a four-element antenna array and Landshield Plus a seven-element array with an integrated anti-jam processor; both use steerable null technology and include spoofing detection. The award follows a 2025 BAE Systems contract in the same category (The Defense Post).

The Netherlands is drafting a procurement model where the government pays commercial firms to stay on call for wartime production. Arms procurement minister Derk Boswijk told reporters: 'We can buy 1 million drones, but I know one thing for sure: that weeks from now they are outdated.' The concept, as he described it, is paying an automaker to develop and prototype drones in peacetime, then convert its line when conflict breaks out. Bell Textron and Lockheed Martin both signed agreements at last week's Netherlands-US defense industry days (Defense One).

The UK is deploying RAF Typhoons to Saudi Arabia for defensive patrols against Houthi missile and drone attacks, plus an A400M for intra-kingdom lift and military advisers. London is extending aerial refueling support for Saudi air operations. The deployment expands an existing British air-defense package, and follows a Yemeni government offensive near the Bab al-Mandab Strait (The Defense Post, citing a UK government operational update).

Oshkosh Defense is building a Vehicle Integration Center to cut modification-testing time from roughly 18 months to weeks, targeting work in 2027. Chief growth officer Logan Jones said the center could serve other vehicle makers and that the industry bottleneck is interface control documentation — 'we don't make that easy today' (Defense One).
sections.whyItMatters: Four different countries are attacking the same underlying gap from four directions: Sweden buying resilience into navigation, the Netherlands buying optionality instead of inventory, Britain buying presence instead of stock, and Oshkosh buying speed in integration. None of it is a weapons program, and all of it is what the last three years of war taught procurement offices.

bottomLine: Thursday's defining move was the F-35 framework: 850 jets, a ten-year horizon, and Lockheed putting $7 billion of its own capital behind a contract Congress has not authorized. That is either the template for how the Pentagon buys at scale from here, or the largest unfunded promise in the current budget cycle — and the Senate NDAA sitting until after the midterms will decide which. Around it, the day showed European buyers moving on their own schedules rather than Washington's: Denmark buying its first retaliatory strike missile, Britain's own defense committee warning that Type 26 exports to Norway could push the Royal Navy's towed-array frigate fleet to 2037, and NATO opening its procurement agency to Ukraine as bilateral US channels wobble. The through-line is not a shift away from American equipment — Denmark is buying an American missile, and the F-35 deal is American — but a shift away from depending on American timelines.
sources: Defense News, Lockheed Martin (news release), US Department of War (release), Government Accountability Office (via Defense News), SAM.gov sources-sought notice (via Defense News), The War Zone (via Defense News), TV2 Denmark (via Defense News), Reuters, The Defense Post, Defense One, Financial Times (via Defense News), UK Parliament Defence Committee report, UK Government operational update
